title: Life Is Asymmetric. The Scientists Who Figured Out Why Won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
gist: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for showing how chemical asymmetry could arise and be amplified, opening routes to controlling reactions used in pharmaceuticals. Kagan's nonlinear effect and Soai's autocatalytic reaction reaching 99.99 percent of one enantiomer realized conditions from Charles Frank's 1953 model.

insights.claim: The 2026 Chemistry Nobel went to Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai for a solution to nature's chemical asymmetry that opened new avenues for manipulating reactions used to make pharmaceuticals and other materials.

insights.claim: Homochirality matters for drugs because one enantiomer gives the therapeutic effect while the other can cause harmful side effects, and chemists cannot always easily control which they get.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Selective synthesis is core to safe drug production.

insights.claim: Charles Frank's 1953 model required an asymmetric reaction, amplification of the imbalance, and autocatalysis in which the product produces the catalyst, creating a positive feedback loop.

insights.claim: Kagan realized the metal catalyst binds both enantiomers, so mixed A-B combinations can slow the reaction and indirectly favor one product, a 'nonlinear effect' that gives a new way to manipulate reactions.

insights.claim: Soai used 5-pyrimidylalkanol to turn a 2 percent initial excess of one enantiomer into 87 percent by reaction end through autocatalysis.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Shows dramatic amplification of tiny asymmetry is achievable.

insights.claim: In 2003 Soai engineered a reaction where a chance tiny imbalance amplified until one enantiomer reached up to 99.99 percent of the product, a feat the Nobel Committee said no one had achieved other than life itself.
insights.speaker: Fernanda González
insights.so_what: Reproduces nature's homochirality in the lab, informing origin-of-life research and chemistry.
